doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Guitars, improvisation and Jimmy McHugh songs
summary: He explains the preparation for each stream, a shift toward improvising on standards like Gershwin, Arlen and Jimmy McHugh tunes, and missing a rhythm section.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I think I was watching when someone wrote in and said, “Well how many guitars do you own?” Answer?

I forget what I answered, as many as I need certainly. But the thing is that kind of this “Moody Monday,” “Wednesday Workshop” and “Finger Buster Friday” each one of those requires that I do work in advance. I kind of identify, okay, when a request comes in and I have to say okay is this something that I’ve already arranged and not played since I recorded it, and then have to revisit that, or is it something that I have to pull out of the hat as it were. But one of the things, you know I spent a lot of time really concentrating on altered tunings and very meticulous arrangements of things. But the counterbalance to that is I’ve spent over the last few years, especially as I’ve done more jazz gigs, a lot more improvisation. And so looking for the opportunity to be able to dive into a Gershwin tune or Harold Arlen tune or something, in a way where I’m not having to also kind of recall the intricacy of an altered tuning arrangement but just be able to be in standard tuning and just go for the gusto. My friend Lee, Lee Newman, is the grandson of Jimmy McHugh, the songwriter. And so I’ve thrown in, on my last “But One” album I did “I Can’t Give You Anything But Love, Baby” and I just, for Lee, recently did a “I’m in the Mood for Love” I did a recording of that for him, and I did “Sunny Side of the Street” too, which are all Jimmy McHugh songs. And I like to be able to kind of pull out something from that era and just be able to launch into the improvisational aspects of it. I miss having a rhythm section, however. But that’s something to be determined. There’s a local studio that I just found out has set it up where each one of its recording rooms is now set up so that each musician can be in their own room and they have linkage between all the different rooms. So even though we couldn’t be on the same stage, we could be performing together and streaming it. So that’s something to consider. But it’s still not the same as having an audience there too, to get that feedback from.
